latent_mechanisms.display_name: Adventitial dendritic cell and T-cell activation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Activation of dendritic cells around the vasa vasorum recruits CD4/CD8 T cells and initiates immune injury in the aortic wall and major branches.
Macrophage-rich granulomatous inflammation involving adventitia, media, and intima of the aorta and major branches; the core tissue lesion of Takayasu arteritis.
IL-6, IL-17, and systemic cytokine signaling drive fever, fatigue, anemia of inflammation, thrombocytosis, CRP elevation, and ESR elevation; levels may be discordant with fixed vascular damage.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Medial elastic lamina destruction and wall weakening
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Giant-cell and macrophage injury fragments elastic laminae and weakens the media, predisposing to dilation, aneurysm, aortic regurgitation, and dissection.
Chronic intimal proliferation and fibrosis narrow arterial lumens, producing pulse deficits, limb claudication, renovascular hypertension, cerebrovascular ischemia, and coronary ostial disease.
Subclavian, carotid, vertebral, or brachiocephalic stenosis causes arm claudication, blood-pressure discrepancy, bruits, visual symptoms, syncope, and stroke hazard.
Renal artery stenosis activates RAAS, driving severe hypertension, renal dysfunction, hypertensive emergency, and downstream cardiac/aortic risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Coronary ostial and proximal coronary arteritis
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Inflammation or fibrotic stenosis of coronary ostia and proximal coronaries produces angina, myocardial ischemia, and acute coronary syndrome hazard.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Aortic root dilation and aortic valve insufficiency
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Ascending aortic/root inflammation and dilation separate valve commissures, causing aortic regurgitation, LV volume overload, heart failure, and surgical hazard.
Pulmonary artery wall inflammation, stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysmal disease can produce dyspnea, hypoxemia, pulmonary hypertension, and right-heart strain.
Takayasu arteritis often relapses or smolders despite clinical improvement; repeated inflammation accelerates fixed stenosis and aneurysmal damage.
High-dose glucocorticoids and steroid-sparing immunosuppressants increase bacterial, viral, TB, and opportunistic infection hazards, especially during induction or biologic therapy.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Adventitial antigen-presenting cells recruit T cells and macrophages that form granulomatous panarteritis.
T-cell and macrophage activation releases IL-6 and related cytokines that drive systemic acute-phase response.
Granulomatous macrophage and giant-cell injury fragments elastic laminae and weakens the aortic media.
Inflamed arterial wall heals with intimal proliferation and fibrosis, producing fixed stenosis and occlusion.
IL-6 is a major hepatic CRP driver in active Takayasu arteritis.
ESR rises with acute-phase proteins and anemia of inflammation, though it can lag CRP.
Systemic cytokine activity produces low-grade fever or febrile constitutional phase.
Fatigue, malaise, and weight loss are common early systemic inflammatory manifestations.
Mural inflammation produces concentric wall thickening on CTA/MRA/ultrasound.
Active macrophage-rich arterial inflammation is FDG-avid on PET/CT.
Intimal proliferation and fibrosis narrow aortic branch lumens.
Subclavian artery stenosis is a classic lesion producing pulse deficit and arm claudication.
Carotid and vertebral branch disease causes cerebral hypoperfusion and stroke risk.
Renal artery stenosis is a major cause of hypertension and renal dysfunction in Takayasu arteritis.
Arch-vessel stenoses translate fixed anatomic narrowing into limb and cerebral hypoperfusion physiology.
Hemodynamically significant subclavian or brachiocephalic stenosis produces weak or absent pulses.
Unilateral proximal subclavian disease lowers distal arm pressure, creating an inter-arm systolic difference.
Arm exertion exposes flow limitation from proximal upper-extremity arterial stenosis.
Carotid/vertebral stenosis or occlusion increases cerebral ischemia and stroke hazard.
Renal hypoperfusion activates RAAS and renovascular hypertension physiology.
RAAS activation drives often severe systolic hypertension.
Bilateral renal artery disease or solitary-kidney stenosis can reduce GFR and raise creatinine.
The same inflammatory-fibrotic remodeling can involve coronary ostia and proximal coronary arteries.
Coronary ostial stenosis can produce exertional or unstable angina.
Critical coronary ostial/proximal stenosis raises MI and unstable ischemia hazard.
Medial weakening and chronic inflammation allow progressive aortic dilation and aneurysm formation.
Ascending aortic and root dilation predispose to aortic regurgitation.
Root dilation is the measurable substrate for annular/commissural separation.
Root dilation and valve involvement cause progressive aortic regurgitation.
Severe aortic regurgitation produces LV volume overload and heart failure hazard.
Takayasu arteritis can involve pulmonary arteries with stenosis or occlusion.
Pulmonary arterial wall inflammation remodels into stenosis/occlusion on CTA/MRA.
Pulmonary artery stenoses increase pulmonary vascular resistance and right-heart load.
Pulmonary vascular limitation and pulmonary hypertension produce exertional dyspnea.
Relapsing or smoldering inflammation adds cumulative fixed vascular damage.
Glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants increase serious and opportunistic infection hazard.
Major stroke directly increases short-term mortality hazard.
Aortic dissection or rupture is an acute high-mortality event.
Takayasu-related coronary ischemia can cause MI, arrhythmia, and death.
Heart failure from aortic regurgitation, hypertension, or ischemia is a major mortality driver.
Treatment-related serious infection and sepsis increase mortality, especially during high-dose steroid exposure.

axes.shape_free_text: Often elevated in active Takayasu arteritis but can be normal despite vascular progression, especially under IL-6 blockade.
Commonly elevated in active disease; slower to rise/fall and less specific than vascular imaging.
Low-grade fever is common in the early systemic inflammatory phase; high fever should also raise infection concern during immunosuppression.
History of recurrent constitutional fever during active inflammatory phase.
Fatigue and malaise are common constitutional manifestations and may persist during active inflammation.
Inflammatory anorexia and catabolism can cause gradual unintentional weight loss.
Mild normocytic anemia of inflammation; severe anemia is not a defining feature and should prompt alternate/additional causes.
Usually normal to mildly elevated in active disease; glucocorticoids can raise neutrophil count.
Reactive thrombocytosis can accompany IL-6-driven active inflammation.
Can be high from renovascular hypertension; readings may be falsely low in an arm supplied by a stenotic subclavian artery.
Often elevated with renal artery stenosis and RAAS activation.
Difference in systolic blood pressure between arms, typically from unilateral subclavian or brachiocephalic stenosis.
Weak or absent radial/brachial pulse from proximal large-vessel stenosis; classic but not universal.
Audible bruit over carotid, subclavian, abdominal aorta, or renal arteries caused by turbulent flow across stenosis.
Exercise-induced arm pain, fatigue, or weakness from subclavian/axillary flow limitation.
Leg claudication from descending aortic, iliac, or femoral large-vessel stenosis; less specific than upper-limb disease.
Tender neck pain over inflamed carotid artery during active disease.
Headache can reflect carotid involvement, hypertension, or cerebral hypoperfusion; nonspecific alone.
Transient visual blurring, amaurosis, or ischemic visual symptoms from carotid/vertebrobasilar disease.
Can reflect coronary ostial stenosis, aortic pathology, or severe hypertension; not specific without vascular/cardiac evidence.
Dyspnea may arise from pulmonary artery stenosis/pulmonary hypertension, aortic regurgitation, heart failure, or anemia.
Concentric mural thickening/edema/enhancement of the aorta or primary branches on ultrasound, CTA, or MRA; marker of mural disease.
Arterial FDG uptake on PET/CT indicating metabolically active large-vessel inflammation; can persist variably after symptom improvement.
Aggregate stenotic burden across major aortic branches; parent-level imaging burden for branch-specific stenosis satellites.
CTA/MRA/ultrasound stenosis or occlusion burden in subclavian arteries.
CTA/MRA/ultrasound stenosis or occlusion burden in carotid/vertebral cerebral supply vessels.
Renal artery stenosis/occlusion burden, usually proximal/ostial, driving renovascular hypertension.
Pulmonary artery stenosis, occlusion, or mural thickening burden on CTA/MRA/perfusion imaging.
Coronary ostial or proximal stenosis burden on coronary CTA/angiography.
Aortic root diameter by echo/CTA/MRA; root dilation predisposes to aortic regurgitation.
Maximal aortic aneurysm diameter across involved segments; late damage marker and dissection/rupture risk driver.
Aortic regurgitation severity by echocardiography, usually from root dilation or valve/root involvement.
May rise with bilateral renal artery stenosis, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, or medication toxicity.
Usually normal unless pulmonary artery disease, pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, or anemia is clinically significant.
Echo/right-heart-catheterization severity of pulmonary hypertension due to pulmonary artery stenosis or chronic pulmonary vascular disease.
Per-day hazard of ischemic stroke from carotid/vertebral stenosis, hypertension, or aortic branch disease.
Per-day hazard of unstable angina or myocardial infarction from coronary ostial/proximal arteritis or severe hypertension.
Per-day hazard of critical limb ischemia from severe subclavian, aortoiliac, or peripheral large-vessel stenosis.
Per-day hazard of hypertensive emergency from renal artery stenosis and severe uncontrolled blood pressure.
Per-day hazard of aortic dissection or rupture in aneurysmal/root disease, especially with uncontrolled hypertension.
Per-day hazard of clinically significant heart failure from aortic regurgitation, severe hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, or coronary ischemia.
Per-day hazard of serious bacterial, viral, TB, or opportunistic infection from immunosuppression.
Aggregate per-day mortality hazard from stroke, aortic dissection/rupture, ACS, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, severe hypertension, and treatment-related infection.
Current uncontrolled serious infection context that changes immunosuppression risk/benefit.
Baseline or treatment-amplified susceptibility to infection, including cumulative steroid/biologic exposure.
Pregnancy or near-term pregnancy planning; modifies drug choice and vascular risk monitoring.
Advanced kidney dysfunction that changes methotrexate, contrast, ACEi/ARB, and procedural risk.
HBsAg or anti-HBc positivity and other HBV reactivation risk context before biologic or cytotoxic immunosuppression.
Baseline and toxicity monitoring axis for methotrexate, azathioprine, leflunomide, tocilizumab, and infection/reactivation contexts.
Treatment safety axis for ACEi/ARB, renal artery stenosis, renal impairment, and TMP-SMX prophylaxis.
Steroid-induced hyperglycemia monitoring axis.
Bone-protection and renal-safety monitoring axis during glucocorticoid exposure, vitamin D supplementation, bisphosphonate use, or renal impairment.
Bleeding hazard relevant to antiplatelet therapy, surgery, and vascular procedures.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both acute-phase markers rise with active inflammation, though ESR lags and is less specific.
Systemic inflammation often tracks vascular PET activity, but discordance is common.
Inflamed thickened arterial wall is often metabolically active on PET, but chronic scar can remain thick without FDG uptake.
Proximal unilateral upper-limb stenosis lowers distal arm pressure.
Flow limitation causes exertional arm ischemia.
Critical carotid or vertebral disease increases cerebral ischemia hazard.
Very high blood pressure increases acute end-organ injury hazard.
Critical coronary ostial stenosis raises ischemia and infarction hazard.
Larger aneurysm diameter increases dissection or rupture hazard.
Uncontrolled hypertension increases wall stress in a weakened aorta.
Severe aortic regurgitation drives LV volume overload and decompensated heart failure.
Pulmonary artery stenosis raises pulmonary vascular resistance.
Pulmonary hypertension can cause right-heart failure and mortality.
Serious infection or sepsis during immunosuppression directly increases mortality hazard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Metabolically active vascular inflammation is the target of systemic anti-inflammatory induction.
Active infection must be treated or excluded because glucocorticoids can mask and worsen infection.

failure_modes: persistent vascular imaging progression despite normalized CRP
treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid induction of remission for active Takayasu arteritis, usually followed by taper and a steroid-sparing agent because relapse and toxicity are common.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pulse steroid may be used when rapidly progressive organ- or life-threatening vascular inflammation coexists with urgent cardiology/vascular management.
Infection risk rises sharply; antimicrobial evaluation and coverage may be needed.

treatments.context_specific_role: Short pulse course for severe active vascular inflammation with threatened organ perfusion; it does not mechanically open established stenoses.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Methotrexate accumulates in renal impairment with marrow and mucosal toxicity.
Methotrexate is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing conventional immunosuppressant for induction/maintenance in non-pregnant patients without severe renal impairment.
Steroid-sparing maintenance option and pregnancy-compatible alternative when other agents are unsuitable.
Steroid-sparing option used in some cohorts, especially when methotrexate or azathioprine is unsuitable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Leflunomide is teratogenic and requires washout for pregnancy planning.
Leflunomide can worsen hypertension, important in renovascular disease.

treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing agent used for relapsing or maintenance Takayasu arteritis in selected patients.
High-intensity option for severe refractory or organ-threatening active disease when other steroid-sparing approaches are inadequate or too slow.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TNF blockade targets macrophage-rich granulomatous large-vessel inflammation.
Biologic TNF blockade should not be started during uncontrolled serious infection.

failure_modes: demyelinating disease or heart failure worsening in susceptible patients

side_effects.interpretation: Serious infection including TB reactivation risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Biologic option for relapsing/refractory active Takayasu arteritis, especially when conventional steroid-sparing agents fail.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: IL-6 blockade can mask fever/CRP and worsen infection.

side_effects.interpretation: Pharmacologic CRP suppression independent of full vascular remission

treatments.context_specific_role: Targeted biologic option for relapsing/refractory active disease or glucocorticoid-sparing therapy; CRP cannot be used alone to monitor activity after initiation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antiplatelet therapy is most relevant when ischemic vascular risk is high.
Bleeding risk can outweigh modest ischemic prophylaxis benefit.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct to reduce arterial ischemic events in high-risk stenotic disease or after vascular intervention, balanced against bleeding risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ACEi/ARB can worsen GFR or potassium in bilateral renal artery stenosis; calcium channel blocker or beta blocker may be safer until anatomy is defined.

failure_modes: AKI or hyperkalemia with RAAS blockade
masked low arm pressure from subclavian stenosis

side_effects.interpretation: Hemodynamic GFR fall, especially with bilateral renal artery stenosis

treatments.context_specific_role: Risk reduction for hypertension-mediated heart failure, stroke, kidney injury, and aortic complications; measure pressure in unaffected limb or leg when needed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Restenosis and procedural failure risk are higher when intervention is performed during active inflammation; urgent ischemia may override delay.

treatments.context_specific_role: Mechanical treatment for critical stenosis causing renovascular hypertension, limb/cerebral ischemia, or coronary compromise; scheduled during quiescent disease when feasible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active inflammation increases anastomotic complications and recurrent dilation risk; urgent dissection or severe heart failure can force surgery.

treatments.context_specific_role: Surgical correction for severe aortic regurgitation, aortic root/ascending aneurysm, dissection, or rupture risk; inflammation control remains important around surgery.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: PJP prophylaxis is relevant during high-dose steroids combined with cytotoxic or biologic immunosuppression.

side_effects.interpretation: Tubular secretion blockade or true renal adverse effect

treatments.context_specific_role: PJP prophylaxis during high-risk immunosuppressive periods, especially high-dose glucocorticoid plus cyclophosphamide or biologic therapy.
Bone protection for prolonged glucocorticoid exposure and chronic inflammatory disease.

age_10_to_40.trajectory_modulation: Peak onset in adolescence and young adulthood; delayed diagnosis allows stenotic damage to accumulate before treatment.

age_over_60.trajectory_modulation: Late presentation is less typical and competing large-vessel diseases become more likely.

female.trajectory_modulation: Marked female predominance in most cohorts; pregnancy planning modifies treatment and hemodynamic monitoring.

asian.trajectory_modulation: Higher incidence and HLA-B52/DRB1*1502 enrichment reported in East Asian cohorts.

latin_american.trajectory_modulation: Higher disease burden reported in several Latin American cohorts compared with northern European populations.

carrier.trajectory_modulation: Associated with Takayasu arteritis susceptibility and sometimes more severe vascular disease in Asian cohorts.

multi_territory_large_vessel_disease.trajectory_modulation: Extensive disease predicts relapse, vascular intervention, ischemic complications, and accumulated damage.

present.trajectory_modulation: Renovascular hypertension is a major morbidity driver and may require revascularization if medically resistant.
Persistent PET/MRI activity, rising symptoms, or prior relapse increases cumulative stenosis/aneurysm risk and need for biologic escalation.

latent_tb.trajectory_modulation: Does not define Takayasu arteritis, but strongly modifies biologic safety and infection hazard.

supportive_care: Baseline mapping of the entire aorta and major branches with CTA or MRA; ultrasound for accessible carotid/subclavian follow-up when expertise exists.
Use PET/CT, contrast MRI, or vessel-wall imaging when symptoms and CRP/ESR are discordant or biologic therapy suppresses acute-phase markers.
Measure blood pressure in both arms and, when upper-limb stenosis makes arm readings unreliable, use the less affected limb or leg pressure strategy consistently.
Aggressive blood pressure control with renal artery anatomy in mind; monitor creatinine and potassium after RAAS blockade.
Regular echocardiography for aortic regurgitation, aortic root dilation, LV function, and pulmonary hypertension when clinically indicated.
Coronary evaluation when chest pain, ischemic ECG/troponin changes, or proximal aortic/root disease suggests coronary ostial involvement.
Vascular surgery/interventional radiology planning for critical stenoses, ideally when disease activity is controlled unless ischemia is urgent.
Vaccination review before immunosuppression: influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, recombinant zoster, HBV when indicated; avoid live vaccines during active immunosuppression.
Screen for latent TB, HBV, HCV, and HIV before biologic or cytotoxic therapy; treat latent TB before TNF blockade when feasible.
Bone protection during glucocorticoids with calcium, vitamin D, DEXA surveillance, and antiresorptive therapy according to fracture risk.
Glucose, blood pressure, weight, mood, and infection surveillance during high-dose glucocorticoid induction.
CBC and liver enzyme monitoring for methotrexate, azathioprine, leflunomide, mycophenolate, tocilizumab, and cyclophosphamide.

Fertility and contraception counseling before methotrexate, mycophenolate, leflunomide, or cyclophosphamide; pregnancy should be coordinated with maternal-fetal medicine, rheumatology, and vascular/cardiology teams.
Avoid elective vascular intervention during active vascular inflammation when possible because restenosis and graft complications are higher.
Smoking cessation, lipid management, exercise rehabilitation, and cardiovascular risk reduction.
Patient education on urgent symptoms: new focal neurologic deficit, syncope, severe chest/back pain, acute dyspnea, limb rest pain, or severe hypertension symptoms.
Longitudinal disease activity tracking should combine symptoms, physical vascular exam, CRP/ESR, and serial imaging rather than any single biomarker.
Multidisciplinary follow-up with rheumatology, vascular medicine/surgery, cardiology, nephrology, radiology, and obstetrics when relevant.
